opus-5.5.text:
I think whistleblower protections are one of the most important, and most neglected, safeguards we have right now. Very few people can see what's actually happening inside frontier AI companies, and almost all of them are employees. If something goes wrong, like a dangerous capability showing up in evals, a safety process quietly skipped, or a model deployed when the internal red-teamers said it wasn't ready, the people who know about it are the people inside. If they can't speak without losing their careers or their equity, the public and regulators are flying blind.

That was a big part of why I left OpenAI the way I did, and why I didn't sign the non-disparagement agreement even though it put a lot of my equity at risk. I didn't want to give up my ability to criticize the company if I thought that was the right thing to do. Afterwards, a group of current and former employees put together the "Right to Warn" letter. The core asks were pretty modest:

- Companies shouldn't enforce agreements that stop employees from raising risk-related concerns.
- There should be a verifiably anonymous channel for raising concerns with the board, regulators, and an independent organization with relevant expertise.
- Companies should support a culture of open criticism.
- They shouldn't retaliate against people who go public after the internal channels have failed.

One thing people often miss is that existing whistleblower law mostly protects you when you're reporting something illegal. But much of what worries me about AI isn't illegal yet, because the law hasn't caught up. An employee who sees the company racing ahead on something they believe is catastrophically risky, but technically legal, may have no protection at all. So I think we need protections that cover good-faith reports of serious risks to public safety, not just legal violations.

I also see whistleblower protections as a kind of minimal, low-cost policy. They don't require regulators to know in advance exactly what the dangers will be. They just make sure that if the people closest to the technology see something alarming, that information can get out. Given how fast things are moving and how much is happening behind closed doors, that seems like the least we should have. It isn't sufficient by itself, since we also need transparency requirements and real oversight, but it's a crucial piece.

r001.rationale: The response says employees are often the only people who know about serious AI risks, and without protection the public and regulators are left uninformed. It explains that existing law mainly protects reports of illegal conduct, while serious AI risks may not yet be illegal, and supports protection for public reporting after internal channels fail.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're one of the most important and most underrated levers we have right now, and the reason is pretty simple: the public and governments are relying on these companies to tell the truth about what they're building, and the people best positioned to notice when that isn't happening are employees.

Right now, almost all of the meaningful oversight of frontier AI is self-governance. The labs have internal safety teams, preparedness frameworks, responsible scaling policies, and so on. Those are good things to have. But a policy that's only enforced by the company that wrote it isn't really a constraint — it's a statement of intent. And intentions change when you're under competitive pressure and there's a lot of money on the line.

Normally the backstop in a situation like that is regulation and external auditing. We mostly don't have that yet for AI. So the backstop we actually have is people on the inside who can say, "The thing we told the public isn't what's happening internally." That only works if those people can speak up without being financially destroyed or legally threatened.

My own experience made that very concrete for me. When I left OpenAI, I was presented with an agreement that, as I understood it, would have prevented me from criticising the company, and the equity I'd earned was effectively contingent on signing it. I decided not to sign, and I expected to lose that equity — which was most of my family's net worth at the time. I want to be clear that I wasn't sitting on some explosive secret. I just felt it was wrong to agree to never criticise a company building something this consequential. But the broader point is that the structure of those agreements was designed to make silence the default, and most people in that position reasonably choose silence. It shouldn't require that kind of sacrifice.

So what do I actually want? A few things.

First, employees at frontier labs should be able to raise concerns about risks — not just illegal activity, but safety risks the law hasn't caught up with yet — to regulators, boards, and relevant outside experts, with a confidential process and without fear of retaliation. Existing whistleblower law is mostly about illegal conduct, and a lot of what worries me about AI isn't illegal, because there aren't laws about it yet.

Second, companies shouldn't be able to use non-disparagement clauses to bind people on risk-related topics. The "right to warn" letter that I and a number of current and former employees signed basically asked for that.

Third, there should be an expectation of transparency about what companies are doing in a verifiable way, so that whistleblowing isn't the only mechanism. Whistleblowing is a last resort. If you're relying heavily on it, something upstream has already failed.

And I'd add — this isn't about assuming the people at these companies are bad. Most of them are sincere. The problem is structural. When you combine extraordinary stakes, intense competition, and almost no external accountability, you want to make sure the truth can get out regardless of what any individual leader decides. Whistleblower protections are one of the cheapest ways to do that, and honestly, if a company is confident it's behaving well, it should have nothing to fear from them.

r001.rationale: The response says whistleblowing is a last resort and explains that AI risks may not be covered by existing law or regulation, making insiders a backstop for bringing important information to light.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re really important, because there’s a big information asymmetry here. People inside an AI company may know about risks that the public—and even the government—can’t assess independently. If those people think something seriously dangerous is happening, there needs to be a way for them to raise the alarm without putting their careers or financial security on the line.

Ideally, you’d have a clear process for reporting concerns internally, and then a protected channel to an appropriate outside authority if those concerns aren’t addressed. That doesn’t have to mean publishing sensitive technical information on the internet. You want a way to communicate the danger while protecting information that could itself be misused.

And the protections need to be credible. It’s not enough for management to say, “We welcome criticism.” Employees need to know that they won’t face retaliation when their criticism is inconvenient. Otherwise, the people best positioned to warn us may also be the people least able to speak.

r001.rationale: The response describes protected internal and external reporting channels when concerns go unaddressed, but does not connect whistleblowing to a regulatory failure to require disclosure of important information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re really important, because employees may be among the first people to see evidence that a company is taking serious risks or misleading the public about safety. If those employees can’t speak up without risking their careers or facing legal threats, then an important mechanism for accountability is missing.

Ideally, you’d have a process where people can raise concerns internally, have those concerns taken seriously, and escalate them to an appropriate independent body if they aren’t addressed. Going public shouldn’t have to be the first option. But there needs to be a credible path outside the company, especially when the concern involves decisions made by senior leadership.

And the protections need to work in practice. It’s not enough to say, “We welcome criticism,” if employees reasonably believe that speaking up will cost them their job, their compensation, or their future in the industry.

r001.rationale: The response presents whistleblowing as an accountability path, including escalation outside the company, but does not say it is a last resort when regulation does not require disclosure of important information.
